A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same privacy-auditing work. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: V1 reports original auditing experiments on CIFAR10 and Housing, synthetic loss-landscape experiments, and appendix analyses of adversary variants and auditing approximations.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds batch-size/noise experiments, a comparator evaluation, unknown-initialization tests, pretrained-model auditing, and privacy-profile results.

M1.justification: Section 6 substantially generalizes the loss-landscape adversary: its gradient function changes from values bounded by C to batch-gradient sums bounded by BC, and updates explicitly divide the gradient sum and noise by B. This changes the modeled dynamics and adversary capabilities. The real-data A_GC-R and A_GC-S procedures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: CIFAR10 and Housing remain the evaluation datasets. V2 adds auditing with unknown initialization, changing the adversary's information-access scenario (Appendix G, Figure 12). ImageNet supplies pretrained AlexNet weights for a CIFAR10 experiment; it is not an additional evaluated benchmark.

E2.justification: Appendix G newly evaluates A_CotS, adapted from Andrew et al. (2024), against the proposed and loss-based adversaries on Housing. Figure 8's caption names A_GC-R while its legend names A_GC-S, but A_CotS participation is clear. The ConvNet/ResNet comparator curves from v1 Figure 5 are absent from the replacement landscape experiments.

E3.justification: The landscape evaluation expands to B in {1,2,4,8,16}, noise parameter σ in {1,...,8}, and trajectories through T=25, introducing the ε25/ε1 ratio. V2 also adds unknown-initialization testing, last-layer fine-tuning of pretrained AlexNet, and full privacy-profile evaluation. The original real-data training settings and Table 2 remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Figures 4 and 14 add systematic batch-size/noise sensitivity analysis central to identifying amplification regimes. Appendix G tests robustness to unknown initialization and examines tightness across privacy profiles. Existing dimension-selection ablations, GDP approximation checks, and threshold-search validation are retained, despite relocation and renumbering.

E5.justification: The 5,000 auditing runs, 95% Clopper-Pearson procedure, Figure 1's 30-run reporting, and Housing repetitions remain unchanged. However, the replacement landscape plots in v2 Figures 4 and 14 omit the explicit five-run averaging statement and variability band accompanying v1 Figure 5. This establishes a reporting change, not fewer actual runs.

E6.justification: New landscape results reveal strong batch-size dependence: v2 Figure 4b reports ε25/ε1 of 0.25 at B=1, σ=8, versus 0.99 at B=16, σ=8. Appendix G adds comparator, initialization, pretrained-model, and privacy-profile findings. These are results under expanded conditions; Figures 1–3 and the retained appendix analyses preserve their earlier plotted data.

T1.justification: Section 6 revises the formal stochastic model through explicit batch averaging and the admissible range g in [-BC,BC], replacing the earlier [-C,C] formulation. Its optimality discussion shifts from a T=2 worst-case conjecture to batch-dependent tightness claims. Appendix A's definitions, lemma, and corollary remain substantively unchanged; no new formal proof establishes the new regime claims.

C1.justification: V1 broadly suggests amplification when insertion is intermittent, even under adversarially chosen loss landscapes. V2 instead claims no amplification for sufficiently large batches relative to noise and restricts the amplification possibility to smaller batches. This substantially revises the abstract, contribution summary, and implications while retaining the every-step no-amplification claim.

C2.justification: V2 explains competing effects of noise and batch size on propagation of the initial private signal, materially narrowing applicability. It adds initialization and pretrained-model interpretations and refines the difficulty of realizing worst-case landscapes in ordinary networks. The federated-learning application discussion is removed. Its prose describing the amplification-ratio trend conflicts with Figure 4b's direction.

D1.justification: V2 documents A_CotS gradient generation and cosine scoring in Algorithms 6–7, identifies ImageNet as public pretraining data, specifies last-layer AlexNet fine-tuning, and describes bisection for privacy-parameter conversion. Existing implementation libraries, hyperparameter table, and approximately 3,500 GPU-hour disclosure are retained.

R1.justification: V2 substantially revises positioning through comparison with Annamalai's concurrent no-amplification result, discussion of Asoodeh and Diaz's constrained nonconvex guarantees, and Feng and Tramèr's privacy-backdoor constructions. These qualify novelty and practical realizability beyond merely adding citations. It also adds black-box auditing literature and removes the federated-learning reference associated with the deleted discussion.

P1.justification: Rewriting concentrates on the abstract, contribution summary, landscape analysis, and discussion, with new remarks and Appendix G. The main section sequence, background, core gradient-crafting descriptions, and much experimental prose remain intact. Citation and heading styles also change.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the main landscape displays with trajectory panels and a numerical heatmap, adds several appendix plots and an algorithm display, and regroups/resizes retained appendix figures. The document template, title block, headings, and figure placement also change substantially. Relocated existing analyses are distinguishable from genuinely new displays.

improvement.justification: The batch-dependent formulation and Figures 4/14 address an important omission in v1's landscape analysis, replacing a broad amplification suggestion with substantially better-supported regime boundaries. New comparator and robustness checks strengthen the empirical assessment. Caption inconsistencies, contradictory ratio wording, and reduced uncertainty reporting for the replacement landscape plots are drawbacks, but do not outweigh this central scientific improvement.
